extracted.intended_audience: students and instructors of elementary Euclidean plane geometry (learners of Book I of Euclid's Elements)
extracted.subtask_description: Statements, constructions, and proofs from Euclid's Elements Book I (Propositions XXIX–XLVIII, corollaries, exercises and examination questions) for constructing and reasoning about lines, triangles, parallelograms, squares and angle relationships.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. XXIX — Right line intersecting two parallel lines (alternate angles, exterior equals corresponding interior, interior on same side sum to two right angles)
rubrics_metrics.description: If a right line (EF) intersects two parallel right lines (AB, CD), it makes: (1) the alternate angles (AGH, GHD) equal; (2) the exterior angle (EGB) equal to the corresponding interior angle (GHD); (3) the two interior angles (BGH, GHD) on the same side equal to two right angles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof by contradiction: assume alternate angles unequal, add adjacent angles, use axiom that sum < or > two right angles implies lines meet; derive contradiction with parallel hypothesis. Also shown by equality chaining using earlier axioms. Exercises given to reprove without a prior proposition and to derive equal intercepts and bisector properties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. XXX — Two lines parallel to same line are parallel
rubrics_metrics.description: If two right lines (AB, CD) are parallel to the same right line (EF), then they are parallel to one another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Draw any secant and compare corresponding/alternate angles using parallels to EF; use Axiom i to conclude equality of angles and therefore parallelism. Short proof via angle equalities when intersected by a common secant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. XXXI — Construction: draw through a given point a line parallel to a given line
rubrics_metrics.description: Problem: Through a given point (C) draw a right line parallel to a given right line (AB).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construction: choose D on AB, join CD and construct an angle at C equal to angle ADC (using angle-construction postulate), producing CE parallel to AB (cites previous proposition). Exercises include related constructions (construct triangle from altitude and base angles, draw a line making a given angle to a given line with two solutions, trisect a segment by the described equilateral-triangle/angle-bisector method, inscribe square in equilateral triangle, and others).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. XXXII — External angle equals sum of two internal nonadjacent angles; sum of triangle angles equals two right angles
rubrics_metrics.description: If any side (AB) of triangle ABC be produced to D, the external angle (CBD) equals the sum of the two internal non-adjacent angles (A, C), and the sum of the three internal angles equals two right angles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof: draw BE parallel to AC; use alternate and corresponding angle equalities to express CBD as sum of A and C; then add ABC to both sides and use prior proposition that adjacent interior + exterior equals two right angles. Corollaries: base angles of isosceles triangle, angle-sum relations between triangles, polygon angle sums, properties of equilateral triangles, and many exercises exploring trisecting, perpendiculars concurrency, bisectors, and loci.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. XXXIII — Connecting adjacent extremities of equal and parallel lines yields equal and parallel segment
rubrics_metrics.description: The right lines (AC, BD) joining the adjacent extremities of two equal and parallel right lines (AB, CD) are equal and parallel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Join BC; using AB parallel CD and AB = CD, triangles ABC and DCB are congruent by two sides and included angle (SAS), giving AC = BD and corresponding angles equal; therefore AC ∥ BD. Exercises include projection equalities and converse relationships about equal projections implying parallelism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. XXXIV — Opposite sides and angles of a parallelogram are equal; a diagonal bisects the parallelogram
rubrics_metrics.description: In a parallelogram, opposite sides (AB, CD; AC, BD) and opposite angles (A, D; B, C) are equal to one another, and either diagonal bisects the parallelogram.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Join BC; show triangles ABC and DCB have equal angles and common side, hence corresponding sides equal. Deduce equalities of sides and angles and that diagonals bisect. Corollaries include right-angle cases, conditions for lozenge, characterizations of parallelograms by side or angle equalities, and many further properties (diagonals bisecting, perpendicular diagonals, etc.). Exercises list many standard parallelogram consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. XXXV — Parallelograms on same base and between same parallels are equal
rubrics_metrics.description: Parallelograms on the same base (BC) and between the same parallels are equal in area.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two proofs: (1) when the opposite sides terminate in same point D, each parallelogram is double the triangle BCD; (2) when they don't, use side-equalities of parallelograms and subtract/add triangular parts to show equality. Observation: introduces algebraic equality (=) versus congruence (≡), and notion of identical equality vs equal area. Exercises and geometric rearrangement argument noted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. XXXVI — Parallelograms on equal bases and between same parallels are equal
rubrics_metrics.description: Parallelograms on equal bases (BC, FG) and between the same parallels are equal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Join BE and CH; use equal base hypothesis and parallelogram side equalities to construct intermediate parallelogram BH equal to both, then deduce BD = FH by equalities and axioms. Exercise: prove without joining BE, CH.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. XXXVII — Triangles on same base and between same parallels are equal
rubrics_metrics.description: Triangles (ABC, DBC) on the same base (BC) and between the same parallels (AD, BC) are equal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Extend AD, construct parallels BE ∥ AC and CF ∥ BD to form parallelograms AEBC and DBCF; since parallelograms on same base between same parallels are equal, their halves (the triangles) are equal. Exercises: many constructions and equal-area consequences follow.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. XXXVIII — Two triangles on equal bases and between same parallels are equal
rubrics_metrics.description: Two triangles on equal bases and between the same parallels are equal (equal area).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use construction similar to Prop. XXXVII: triangles are halves of equal parallelograms on equal bases between same parallels. Exercises include medians, area-equality between triangles with supplementary contained angles, and many partition/ratio problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. XXXIX — Equal triangles on same base and same side are between same parallels
rubrics_metrics.description: Equal triangles (BAC, BDC) on the same base (BC) and on the same side of it are between the same parallels (i.e., the lines joining their other vertices are parallel to the base).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof by contradiction: join AD; if AD not parallel to BC, construct AE ∥ BC meeting BD in E, then derive a 'part equal to whole' contradiction via equal-area results. This forces AD ∥ BC.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. XL — Equal triangles on equal bases and forming parts of same right line are between same parallels
rubrics_metrics.description: Equal triangles (ABC, DEF) on equal bases (BC, EF) which form parts of the same right line, and on the same side of the line, are between the same parallels.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Join AD and argue by contradiction: if AD not parallel to BF, construct AG ∥ AD and show via equal-base/parallel properties that a part equals the whole, contradiction, hence AD ∥ BF.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. XLI — Parallelogram on same base and between same parallels is double triangle on same base
rubrics_metrics.description: If a parallelogram (ABCD) and a triangle (EBC) are on the same base (BC) and between the same parallels, the parallelogram is double of the triangle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Join AC. Parallelogram ABCD is double triangle ABC; triangle ABC equals triangle EBC (from previous proposition), hence parallelogram is double triangle EBC. Corollaries relate area relations with bases and altitudes and sums of triangles in a parallelogram.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. XLII — Construct parallelogram equal to a given triangle and having an angle equal to a given angle
rubrics_metrics.description: To construct a parallelogram equal to a given triangle (ABC) and having an angle equal to a given angle (D).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construction: bisect AB at E, join EC, make angle BEF equal to D, draw CG ∥ AB and BG ∥ EF; EG is the required parallelogram. Proof uses equality of triangles from bisection and parallelogram area halving. Exercises follow.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. XLIII — Parallelograms formed by parallels through a point in a diagonal produce equal complements
rubrics_metrics.description: Parallels (EF, GH) through any point (K) in one diagonal (AC) of a parallelogram divide it into four parallelograms, of which the two (BK, KD) through which the diagonal does not pass (the complements) are equal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use that diagonal bisects parallelograms and equalities of component triangles; subtract equal triangle sums to show DK = KB. Corollaries: characterizations of when a point lies on diagonal, equalities among complements, and connections to statics. Exercises include concurrency results and midpoint collinearity of diagonals in quadrilaterals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. XLIV — Apply a parallelogram equal to a given triangle to a given line and with angle equal to given angle
rubrics_metrics.description: To apply to a given right line (AB) a parallelogram equal to a given triangle (C) and have one of its angles equal to a given angle (D).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct parallelogram BEFG equal to triangle C with angle B equal to D and side BE on AB; through A draw AH ∥ BG and extend FG to meet AH at H; produce constructions and use parallel-angle-sum arguments plus axiom about lines meeting when angle sums differ from two right angles to find point K and draw KL ∥ AB producing the required parallelogram AM equal to the triangle. Full dem. included. Exercises: construct rectangles equal to sums/differences of figures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. XLV — Construct a parallelogram equal to a given rectilineal figure and have angle equal to given angle
rubrics_metrics.description: To construct a parallelogram equal to a given rectilineal figure (ABCD) and having an angle equal to a given rectilineal angle (X).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Divide the figure into triangles via a diagonal BD, construct parallelograms for each triangle equal to them and with angle X, then join; prove sides align and resultant EI is parallelogram equal to ABCD. Suggestion: easier when framed as constructing rectangles. Exercises on constructing rectangles equal to sums/differences of figures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. XLVI — Construct a square on a given straight line
rubrics_metrics.description: On a given right line (AB) to describe a square.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct perpendicular AD at B (or erect at A), make AD = AB, draw DC ∥ AB and BC ∥ AD to form square AC. Proof uses parallelogram and equality of sides to show all four sides equal and one angle right. Exercises explore properties of squares and related regular polygons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. XLVII — Pythagoras: square on hypotenuse equals sum of squares on other two sides
rubrics_metrics.description: In a right-angled triangle (ABC) the square on the hypotenuse (AB) is equal to the sum of the squares on the other two sides (AC, BC).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof constructs squares on each side, draws parallels to relate component parallelograms and triangles, then uses equality of triangles and doubles to show whole square equals sum of two squares. An alternative orientation-based proof is given; many exercises follow including algebraic identities and derived geometric consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. XLVIII — Converse of Pythagoras: if square on one side equals sum of squares on others, the opposite angle is right
rubrics_metrics.description: If the square on one side (AB) of a triangle equals the sum of the squares on the remaining sides (AC, CB), then the angle (C) opposite that side is a right angle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Direct proof: erect CD at right angle to CB and make CD = CA, join BD and use equal-square sums to deduce AB = BD and then triangle congruence to show angle C is right. Also provides an indirect proof variant by contradiction referencing earlier propositions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition — Altitude of a triangle
rubrics_metrics.description: The altitude of a triangle is the perpendicular from the vertex on the base.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used in exercises and constructions involving areas and relations of triangles and parallelograms (e.g., triangles/parallelograms with equal bases and altitudes are equal).

rubrics_metrics.name: Questions for Examination on Book I — list of key concepts and questions students must master
rubrics_metrics.description: A list of examination-style questions and short-answer prompts covering definitions (geometry, geometric magnitude), primary concepts (points, lines, surfaces), classifications (lines, surfaces), constructions (how many conditions to construct a line or circle), properties (plane geometry scope, subject-matter of Book I), proof methods (direct vs indirect), definitions (adjacent/exterior/interior/alternate angles, projection, medians), and identification of propositions and their relationships.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The examination questions enumerate the expected knowledge for Book I: definitions, basic constructions (conditions needed), classification of problems in Book I, understanding of number of conditions for circles/lines, obverse/identity notions, congruence vs equality, and listing/relating propositions. Useful as a syllabus/checklist for student mastery and revision.
